title: Pro-C groups
summary: The library studies profinite groups through their finite quotients, providing ways to construct maps, determine the ranks of open subgroups, and prove that presented groups are infinite.
overview: A pro-C group is built from finite groups in a chosen class C by taking inverse limits. The selected results explain structural consequences: open subgroups of finite-rank free pro-C groups are free with an explicit rank formula, and a topological generator together with finite quotients of every order characterizes the profinite integers.

Fox derivatives and Crowell exact sequences express relations in modules, while a weighted Golod–Shafarevich criterion detects infinite pro-p groups. For profinite abelian groups, continuous characters recover the original group through Pontryagin biduality. The individual results specify the closure assumptions on C and the groups involved.
scopeNote: This is a selection, not a claim that every theorem about pro-C groups has been formalized. Closure assumptions on C vary by result. The open-subgroup theorem has a finite basis, and the completed Crowell theorem uses a finite-rank free pro-C source and a separated completed differential module. The duality entry concerns profinite abelian groups, not all locally compact abelian groups.

entries.title: Open subgroups of free pro-C groups: freeness and Schreier rank
entries.summary: An open subgroup of a finite-rank free pro-C group is free, with the expected index-dependent rank.
statement: Assume $C$ is closed under isomorphisms, subgroups, quotients, finite direct products, and extensions, and contains a nontrivial finite cyclic group. Let $F$ be epimorphically free pro-$C$ on a finite converging basis $X$, and let $H\le F$ be open. Put $r=|X|$ and $i=[F:H]$.

There is a free pro-$C$ group with a basis of size $$\begin{cases}0,&r=0,\\1+i(r-1),&r\ge1,\end{cases}$$ and a continuous group isomorphism from that group to $H$. The conclusion provides freeness as well as a numerical rank.
discussion: Openness gives finite index, and the rank formula measures exactly how passing to the subgroup changes the number of free generators. The assumptions on C ensure that this process preserves freeness. This is the profinite counterpart of the classical Schreier formula for free groups, developed in the pro-C setting in Ribes and Zalesskii’s monograph.
history: This is the profinite counterpart of the classical Schreier formula for finite-index subgroups of free groups. Ribes and Zalesskii’s monograph develops the free pro-C version, where restrictions on the class of finite groups determine whether the subgroup remains free.

entries.title: Fox’s fundamental formula for group rings
entries.summary: A group-ring boundary decomposes into Fox derivatives times the boundaries of the generators.
statement: Let $X$ be finite, $F(X)$ the free group on $X$, $H$ any group, and $\psi:F(X)\to H$ a homomorphism. For every $w\in F(X)$, $$[\psi(w)]-1=\sum_{x\in X}\frac{\partial_\psi w}{\partial x}\bigl([\psi(x)]-1\bigr)\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z[H].$$ Here $[h]$ denotes the group-ring basis element indexed by $h$, and the derivative is the relative Fox derivative.
The factors occur in the displayed order. The group ring need not be commutative, so exchanging a derivative with the factor to its right changes the assertion.
discussion: In a presentation, a relator maps to the identity and has zero boundary, so its Fox vector lies in the kernel of a linear map over the group ring. This makes noncommutative relations accessible to module calculations. Fox introduced the calculus in his 1953 paper, following his study of Alexander’s knot polynomial; Crowell later developed its connection with derived modules.
history: Fox’s 1953 paper introduced free differential calculus in the free group ring. The subject grew out of his study of Alexander’s knot polynomial. Crowell’s 1971 derived-module construction subsequently gave a universal module interpretation of the associated presentation matrices and exact sequences, connecting the calculus with the homology of covering spaces.

entries.title: Crowell’s exact sequence for a group quotient
entries.summary: A surjective group homomorphism yields an exact sequence connecting its kernel to its derived module.
statement: Let $\psi:G\twoheadrightarrow H$ be a surjective homomorphism of groups and let $N=\ker\psi$. Write $A_\psi$ for the universal module of $\psi$-crossed homomorphisms. Then $$0\longrightarrow N^{\mathrm{ab}}\longrightarrow A_\psi\longrightarrow\mathbb Z[H]\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0$$ is exact.

The head map sends the class of $n$ to its universal differential; the next map sends the differential of $g$ to $[\psi(g)]-1$. The last map is augmentation. The action of $H$ on $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$ comes from conjugation through lifts in $G$.
discussion: Exactness identifies the differentials with zero boundary and shows that every element of the augmentation ideal is a boundary. For a finite-rank free source, Fox coordinates turn these maps into calculations with a presentation. Crowell’s 1971 paper constructed the derived module by a universal property and developed its exact sequence, motivated in part by Alexander modules and knot groups.
history: Crowell’s 1971 paper defines the derived module of a homomorphism by a universal property and constructs its module sequence. The motivation includes Alexander modules and knot groups, but the construction applies to general group homomorphisms. Fox derivatives provide coordinates when a free presentation is available.

entries.title: The completed Crowell exact sequence for free pro-C groups
entries.summary: The kernel–differential–augmentation sequence is exact in the stated finite-rank pro-C setting.
statement: Let $C$ satisfy the source’s full-formation assumptions and contain trivial quotients. The formation package includes closure under quotients, finite subdirect products, normal subgroups, extensions, and subgroups. Let $F$ be a free pro-$C$ group with a chosen converging basis of finite cardinality $r$, and let $\psi:F\twoheadrightarrow H$ be a continuous surjection to a profinite group.

For $N=\ker\psi$, the separated completed differential module gives $$0\to N/\overline{[N,N]}\to A^{\mathrm{sep}}_\psi(C)\to\mathbb Z_C\mathopen{[\![} H\mathclose{]\!]}\to\mathbb Z_C\to0.$$ The bundled endpoint records exactness of the underlying integer-linear maps.

Here $\mathbb Z_C$ is the pro-$C$ completion of the additive group $\mathbb Z$, with its induced ring structure, and $\mathbb Z_C\mathopen{[\![} H\mathclose{]\!]}$ is the corresponding completed group algebra.
discussion: The kernel is abelianized by taking its quotient by the closure of its commutator subgroup. A separated completed differential module then connects this topological quotient to the completed group algebra under the stated assumptions on C. Crowell’s discrete module sequence supplies the algebraic pattern; the profinite version retains compatible information from finite continuous quotients.
history: Crowell’s discrete module sequence provides the algebraic pattern. Profinite group theory, as developed in Ribes and Zalesskii, replaces discrete quotients and modules with objects controlled by finite continuous quotients. The sequence here combines that viewpoint with completed Fox calculus; its hypotheses specify the setting in which the classical pattern remains exact.

entries.title: Golod–Shafarevich: a depth criterion for infinite pro-p groups
entries.summary: A nonpositive presentation polynomial certifies that an actual pro-p group is infinite.
statement: Let $p$ be prime and let $G$ be a profinite group with a displayed finite pro-$p$ presentation on $d$ generators and $r$ relators. For each relator choose a lower Zassenhaus depth $\nu_i$, and assume those depth bounds hold for the displayed presentation. No minimality assumption is required.

If some real $t$ satisfies $0\le t<1$ and $$1-dt+\sum_{i=1}^{r}t^{\nu_i}\le0,$$ then $G$ is infinite. The theorem takes an actual presentation object, not merely numerical values for $d$, $r$, and the depths.
discussion: Relator depths matter because deep relations contribute little to the polynomial, allowing extra conditions to be imposed while preserving infinitude. Countably many added relations also require a limiting argument. Golod and Shafarevich’s 1964 paper established infinite class field towers through generator–relation inequalities; retaining individual depths makes that method useful for constructions with additional splitting conditions.
history: Golod and Shafarevich’s 1964 paper established the existence of infinite class field towers through inequalities for generators and relations. Weighted versions retain the filtration depths of individual relators instead of using only their number. That extra information is what makes it possible to impose carefully chosen deep relations while preserving infinitude.

entries.title: Pontryagin biduality for profinite abelian groups
entries.summary: Evaluation identifies a profinite abelian group with its continuous character bidual.
statement: Let $G$ be a compact, totally disconnected abelian topological group. Its Pontryagin dual $G^\vee$ consists of continuous circle-valued characters with the compact-open topology. The source constructs a continuous group isomorphism $$G\xrightarrow{\sim}(G^\vee)^\vee,\qquad g\longmapsto\bigl(\chi\longmapsto\chi(g)\bigr).$$
This is an isomorphism of the actual topological groups. In particular, finite torsion is retained; this is not an identification obtained only after tensoring with a field.
discussion: Finite quotient characters distinguish elements, while compactness allows compatible finite evaluation conditions to be solved simultaneously. The resulting identification preserves both topology and finite torsion, giving a canonical passage between a group and its character data. This is the profinite abelian case of the duality theory developed in Pontrjagin’s 1934 paper on topological commutative groups.
history: Pontrjagin’s 1934 paper developed the duality theory of topological commutative groups. Character groups provide a common language for finite abelian duality and its topological extensions. The result here is the profinite abelian case of that theory, where finite quotient duality and compactness supply the bidual identification.

entries.title: When a procyclic group is the group of profinite integers
entries.summary: A topological generator and finite quotients of every order characterize the additive group of profinite integers.
statement: Let $G$ be a profinite group and let $g\in G$ topologically generate it. Suppose that for every positive integer $n$ there is an open normal subgroup $U\trianglelefteq G$ with $|G/U|=n$. Then there is a continuous group isomorphism $$G\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat{\mathbb Z}$$ sending $g$ to the compatible residue class of the integer $1$.

The Lean target is the all-finite-groups integer inverse-limit carrier, written multiplicatively to match the source group API. Its distinguished element is additive integer one, not the additive identity of $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$.
discussion: Procyclicity alone is insufficient: finite cyclic groups and p-adic integers also have topological generators, but lack quotients of some orders. Sending the chosen generator to one makes the cyclic quotient coordinates compatible. Ribes and Zalesskii’s 2010 monograph places the profinite integers within procyclic group theory, where they are distinguished by having finite cyclic quotients of every positive order.
history: Procyclic groups form a basic part of the structure theory presented in Ribes and Zalesskii’s 2010 monograph. The profinite integers occupy the universal position among them: their finite cyclic quotients range over all positive orders. The recognition theorem expresses that role using a chosen generator.
